right: Someone is talking on the phone next to me.
My cat is sleeping on the sofa.
I'm reading a book about space this month.
I'm trying to go to bed earlier these days.

wrong.text: Listen! Somebody knocks at the door.
wrong.why: 'Listen!' shows it is happening now, so: is knocking.

wrong.text: Our company doesn't do very well this year.
wrong.why: 'This year' is a period around now, so: isn't doing.

wrong.text: I didn't enjoy my course at first, but I start to like it now.
wrong.why: The change is happening now: I am starting to like it.

right: My father drinks tea after every meal.
My sister never answers her phone.
Most shops in my town close at eight.
It rarely snows in my country.

wrong.text: My sister study medicine in Prague.
wrong.why: she + studies (y changes to -ies).

wrong.text: He doesn't likes spicy food.
wrong.why: After doesn't the verb has no -s.

wrong.text: How much do it cost to fly to Rome?
wrong.why: 'It' takes does.

wrong.text: I am promising I'll call you tonight.
wrong.why: I promise, not I am promising.

right: I usually cook at home, but this week I'm eating out.
I normally work in the office, but today I'm working from home.
My brother is always borrowing my charger.
I'm always forgetting people's names.

wrong.text: I usually am going to work by bike.
wrong.why: 'Usually' describes a habit: I usually go.

wrong.text: The river Nile is flowing into the Mediterranean.
wrong.why: A permanent fact: flows.

wrong.text: Dan is always walking to school. It takes him ten minutes.
wrong.why: A neutral routine, not a complaint: always walks.

right: I prefer cold weather to hot weather.
I don't understand people who hate music.
I'm thinking of buying a bike.
We're having lunch on the balcony.

wrong.text: She is wanting to speak to the manager.
wrong.why: 'Want' is a state verb: she wants.

wrong.text: I am having two sisters and a brother.
wrong.why: have = possess is a state: I have.

wrong.text: Mmm, the bread is smelling wonderful.
wrong.why: 'Smell' stays simple: smells wonderful.

wrong.text: I am hearing somebody at the door.
wrong.why: With hear we use can: I can hear.

right: I went to the lake with my friends.
I bought a new pair of trainers.
I didn't watch any videos yesterday.
I didn't go to the gym because I was tired.

wrong.text: We buyed a new sofa last weekend.
wrong.why: buy is irregular: bought.

wrong.text: Did you saw the match last night?
wrong.why: After did the verb is in its base form: see.

wrong.text: She didn't came to work on Monday.
wrong.why: After didn't the verb is in its base form: come.

wrong.text: Did you be at the meeting yesterday?
wrong.why: No did with be: Were you at the meeting?

right: At eight o'clock yesterday evening I was cooking pasta.
I was watching a series with my sister.
I dropped my phone while I was getting off the bus.
I was walking home when it started to rain.

wrong.text: At 9 pm I watched a film, so I didn't hear the phone.
wrong.why: At 9 pm the film was in progress: was watching.

wrong.text: I was breaking a plate while I was doing the washing-up.
wrong.why: Breaking the plate was the short event: broke.

wrong.text: I was enjoying the concert, but Lisa was wanting to leave.
wrong.why: 'Want' is a state verb: wanted.

right: I've already had breakfast, but I haven't checked my email yet.
I've already been to the gym, but I haven't called my mum yet.
My sister has just passed her driving test.
I've just found a great flat near the park.

wrong.text: The neighbours have move to another city.
wrong.why: After have we need the past participle: moved.

wrong.text: The taxi is arrived. Are you ready?
wrong.why: The present perfect is formed with have / has, not with be: has arrived.

wrong.text: I've yet spoken to the manager, so she knows about the problem.
wrong.why: In a positive sentence we use already (or just), not yet.

right: I've never been to Japan, but I'd love to go.
I've never tried surfing, but I want to learn.
I've been to the gym twice this week.
I've cooked dinner three times so far this week.

wrong.text: Has your sister ever work in a restaurant?
wrong.why: has + ever + past participle: worked.

wrong.text: I don't see Nadia this week. Is she ill?
wrong.why: 'This week' is not finished, so we look back with the present perfect.

wrong.text: Hi, I'm home! I've gone to the hairdresser's.
wrong.why: The speaker is back home, so: been to.

right: I've been learning English for three years.
I've been going to the same gym since January.
I'm tired because I've been studying all day.
My legs hurt because I've been running.

wrong.text: Somebody has being cooking fish in here. I can smell it.
wrong.why: have / has + been + -ing: has been cooking.

wrong.text: I am studying here since September.
wrong.why: 'Since September' covers the time up to now, so: have been studying.

wrong.text: My sister is learning Italian for two years.
wrong.why: 'For two years' up to now needs has been learning, not is learning.

right: I've been running since March, and I've done two races.
I've been learning the guitar for a year, and I've learnt six songs.
I've had this phone for three years.
I've known my best friend since we were six.

wrong.text: Oh no, I've been breaking your favourite glass!
wrong.why: One completed action with a result takes the simple form: have broken.

wrong.text: I've been writing five emails since lunch.
wrong.why: A number of finished things (five emails) takes the simple form: have written.

wrong.text: I've been knowing Pedro for a long time.
wrong.why: know is a state verb, so no -ing: have known.

right: I've lived in this flat for four years.
I've been living in my town since 2019.
I've been a student at this college since September.
I've been a member of the chess club for two years.

wrong.text: I am here since eight o'clock.
wrong.why: 'Since eight o'clock' = from then until now: have been.

wrong.text: My brother works for the same firm since 2019.
wrong.why: 'Since 2019' = from then until now, so the present perfect.

wrong.text: How long do you know Mr Sato?
wrong.why: How long up to now needs the present perfect: have you known.

right: I've had my phone for two years. I've had it since 2024.
I've played football for ten years. I've played since I was eight.
It's two years since I last went to the dentist.
It's ages since I last rode a bike.

wrong.text: I've had this cough since two weeks.
wrong.why: Two weeks is a length of time, so: for.

wrong.text: It's a long time for we ate out together.
wrong.why: It's a long time since + past simple.

wrong.text: They have opened this café three weeks ago.
wrong.why: ago marks a finished time, so the past simple: opened.

right: I've started a pottery class. A colleague told me about it.
My brother has moved to Porto. He found a job there in the spring.
I lost my bank card, but the café kept it for me.
My laptop stopped working, but my cousin repaired it.

wrong.text: The taxi is arrived, so grab your coat.
wrong.why: The present perfect is made with have / has, not with be: has arrived.

wrong.text: The dinosaurs have died out millions of years before humans appeared.
wrong.why: A finished event in the distant past takes the past simple.

wrong.text: Tom has passed his exam! He has heard the result as soon as he woke up.
wrong.why: The details of the news (when and how) go in the past simple.

right: I went to the mountains two years ago.
We visited my aunt in Leeds last August.
I've walked more than ten kilometres this week.
I haven't spoken to my parents today.

wrong.text: My brother has passed his driving test in March.
wrong.why: 'In March' is a finished time: past simple, not present perfect.

wrong.text: When have you moved to this neighbourhood?
wrong.why: 'When…?' needs the past simple: When did you move?

wrong.text: It's nearly midnight. I have spoken to my landlord this morning.
wrong.why: At midnight the morning is finished, so use the past simple.

right: When I got to the party, most of the guests had gone home.
When I reached the stop, my bus had already left.
I was excited because I had never seen the sea before.
I didn't know what to order because I had never eaten Thai food before.

wrong.text: The floor was wet because someone has spilt a drink.
wrong.why: We are looking back from a past moment (was wet), so: had spilt.

wrong.text: I didn't recognise the song because I haven't heard it before.
wrong.why: The main verb is past (didn't recognise), so we look back with hadn't.

wrong.text: She picked up the phone, had dialled the number and waited.
wrong.why: Actions that follow each other in a story are all in the past simple.

right: I was out of breath because I had been running for the bus.
My hands were dirty because I had been planting flowers.
I had been waiting for an hour when the doctor finally called me in.
We had been saving for two years when we bought the car.

wrong.text: Lena was sunburnt because she has been lying on the beach.
wrong.why: We look back from a past moment (was sunburnt), so: had been lying.

wrong.text: We have been driving for three hours when the engine started smoking.
wrong.why: The driving continued up to a past moment (started smoking), so: had been driving.

wrong.text: When I arrived, Tom was waiting for two hours and he looked annoyed.
wrong.why: How long up to a past moment needs had been + -ing, not was + -ing.

wrong.text: I had been knowing Rosa for a year when she introduced me to her family.
wrong.why: Know is a state verb, so it is not used in the continuous: had known.

right: I've got a bike, but I haven't got a car.
We've got a small kitchen, but we haven't got a dishwasher.
I always have a shower before I have breakfast.
I usually have a cup of tea when I get home.

wrong.text: Every room in the hotel have got a kettle.
wrong.why: 'Every room' is singular, so: has got.

wrong.text: My brother doesn't has a driving licence.
wrong.why: After doesn't the verb is the base form: doesn't have.

wrong.text: I have got a shower every morning before work.
wrong.why: Have a shower is an action, so got is not possible.

right: I used to share a room with my sister, but now I live alone.
I used to hate running, but now I do it three times a week.
I didn't use to like mushrooms, but now I cook them all the time.
I didn't use to listen to jazz.

wrong.text: People used to wrote letters much more often.
wrong.why: After used to we need the base verb: used to write.

wrong.text: Did you use to played chess with your dad?
wrong.why: After use to the verb is the base form: use to play.

wrong.text: I use to get up at six every day because my job starts early.
wrong.why: Used to has no present form: for a present habit say I usually get up.

wrong.text: We used to go to the cinema three times last month.
wrong.why: A number of times in a finished period takes the past simple.

right: I'm meeting my cousin for lunch on Saturday.
We're having a team dinner on Friday evening.
My first class starts at 8.30 tomorrow.
The last bus home leaves at 11.20.

wrong.text: Do you come to the cinema with us tonight?
wrong.why: A personal plan for tonight takes the present continuous, not do: Are you coming?

wrong.text: What time is the next bus leave?
wrong.why: With a base verb the question needs does: What time does the next bus leave?

wrong.text: We don't go away this summer because we're saving for a car.
wrong.why: A personal plan takes the present continuous: we aren't going away.

right: I'm going to start running before work.
I'm going to visit my grandmother next weekend.
I was going to cook, but I got home too late.
We were going to go camping, but the car broke down.

wrong.text: We're going to moving house in the spring.
wrong.why: After going to, use the base verb: move.

wrong.text: The baby looks very tired. She going to fall asleep any minute.
wrong.why: going to needs am / is / are: she is going to fall asleep.

wrong.text: We are going to eat out last night, but every restaurant was full.
wrong.why: 'Last night' is past and the plan failed: were going to.

right: Don't worry, I'll lend you my phone.
Shall I call your mum for you?
I'll finish the report before lunch, I promise.
I won't forget your book again.

wrong.text: Is that the last bus? Wait, I come with you!
wrong.why: A sudden decision needs will, not the present simple.

wrong.text: Don't worry about the washing-up. I do it later.
wrong.why: An offer needs will: I'll do it later.

wrong.text: You've been driving for hours. Do I drive for a while?
wrong.why: An offer to do something is Shall I…?, not Do I…?

right: I think I'll live in another country.
I'm sure my English will be much better.
My brother will probably sleep until noon.
My friend Dina probably won't go out.

wrong.text: Don't touch that dog. I'm sure it bites you.
wrong.why: A prediction after I'm sure needs will, not the present simple.

wrong.text: I am not think the shop will be open on Sunday.
wrong.why: The negative of I think is I don't think.

wrong.text: I can't babysit tonight. I will go to a concert with Yusuf, and we've already paid.
wrong.why: The tickets are paid for, so it is arranged: present continuous, not will.

right: I'm going to visit my cousin in Porto.
I'm going to start a photography course.
I'll make you a sandwich.
Wait here. I'll run to the shop.

wrong.text: I can't lend you the car tonight. I will take Mum to the airport, and she's expecting me.
wrong.why: It was decided earlier and Mum is expecting it: going to, not will.

wrong.text: Open the window, please. I feel so dizzy. I will faint.
wrong.why: The speaker can feel it happening now, so: going to.

wrong.text: I've taken tomorrow off because I will help my sister move house.
wrong.why: Taking the day off shows the decision was made earlier: going to.

right: This time tomorrow I'll be sitting in a meeting.
This time tomorrow I'll be walking my dog.
By the end of the year I'll have read twenty books.
By December I'll have finished my course.

wrong.text: Come before eight, because at eight we will watching the final.
wrong.why: will be + -ing: we will be watching.

wrong.text: By the time you wake up, I will have went to work.
wrong.why: After will have, use the past participle: gone.

wrong.text: I can't wait! This time tomorrow I'll have sat on the plane to Cairo.
wrong.why: 'This time tomorrow' is a moment in the middle of the flight: will be + -ing.

right: As soon as I get home, I'll take a shower.
I'll cook dinner when I get home.
If it's sunny, I'll go cycling by the river.
If it rains, I'll stay in and watch a film.

wrong.text: We'll have dinner when Dad will come home.
wrong.why: After when: present simple, not will.

wrong.text: Text me when you will have landed, please.
wrong.why: After when: present perfect, not will have.

wrong.text: If it will be sunny on Sunday, we'll have a barbecue.
wrong.why: After if: present simple, not will.

right: I could ride a bike, but I couldn't swim.
When I was seven, I couldn't tie my shoelaces.
My phone died, but I managed to find the way home.
The queue was huge, but we were able to get tickets.

wrong.text: I would love to can speak Italian like you.
wrong.why: After to we need an infinitive, and can has none: to be able to.

wrong.text: My dad can play the violin when he was at school.
wrong.why: 'When he was at school' is the past, so: could.

wrong.text: The current was strong, but in the end Lucas could pull the boy out.
wrong.why: He succeeded on one occasion, so: was able to or managed to, not could.

right: We could walk along the river and have lunch at the market.
You could visit the old castle on Saturday morning.
I could have joined the choir, but I was too shy.
We could have gone to Norway, but we stayed at home.

wrong.text: I'm so tired today that I can sleep for a whole week.
wrong.why: This is exaggerated, not real, so we use could, not can.

wrong.text: I had a free day yesterday. I could go to the beach, but I stayed in.
wrong.why: 'Yesterday' and 'but I stayed in' show a past chance not taken: could have gone.

wrong.text: Luckily we stayed at home. We couldn't had enjoyed a picnic in that storm.
wrong.why: After couldn't we always use have, never had: couldn't have enjoyed.

right: She must be busy at work today.
His phone can't be switched on.
My brother must have borrowed my laptop.
The cat can't have opened the fridge by itself.

wrong.text: You've been travelling all day. You can't be tired.
wrong.why: A whole day of travelling makes tiredness certain, so: must be.

wrong.text: There was no reply when I knocked. They must had gone out.
wrong.why: After must we always use have, never had: must have gone.

wrong.text: Rosa isn't answering. She must to be in the shower.
wrong.why: Must is followed by the base verb, without to.

right: She might be ill today.
He may be working from home.
I might have left my umbrella in the café.
My sister may have taken my charger.

wrong.text: Try the other entrance. This one maybe closed.
wrong.why: After the subject 'this one' we need a verb: may be, two words.

wrong.text: Her phone was off all morning. She might has forgotten to charge it.
wrong.why: After a modal verb we always use have, never has.

wrong.text: Call her later. She could to be driving now.
wrong.why: Could, like may and might, is followed by the base verb without to.

right: I might go cycling if the weather is good.
We may visit my aunt on Sunday.
The match is cancelled, so I might as well do my homework.
We have an hour to wait, so we might as well have a coffee.

wrong.text: Be careful with that glass. You might to cut yourself.
wrong.why: Might is followed by the base verb, without to.

wrong.text: Start the meeting without me. I might being stuck in traffic at nine.
wrong.why: After might we need the base verb: might be.

wrong.text: It's nearly midnight, so you might so well stay the night.
wrong.why: The phrase is might as well.

right: I have to be at my desk by nine every morning.
We have to switch off our phones in class.
You mustn't let the cat out, but you don't have to take your shoes off.
You don't have to bring a towel, but you mustn't smoke inside.

wrong.text: Did you had to show your passport at the hotel?
wrong.why: After did the verb is in its base form: did you have to.

wrong.text: I must work late last night, so I missed the film.
wrong.why: 'Last night' is the past, so: had to.

wrong.text: Visitors don't have to touch the paintings. It is strictly forbidden.
wrong.why: Forbidden = mustn't. Don't have to would mean it is not necessary.

right: In our library you mustn't eat, but you needn't whisper in the café area.
At my gym you mustn't wear outdoor shoes, but you needn't bring a towel.
I needn't have printed my ticket because they scanned my phone.
I needn't have hurried. The bus was late anyway.

wrong.text: Visitors mustn't to feed the animals in this park.
wrong.why: After mustn't we use the base verb without to.

wrong.text: The station is two minutes away on foot, so we mustn't take a taxi.
wrong.why: A taxi is not forbidden, only unnecessary: needn't.

wrong.text: The exam was cancelled, so I needn't have study all weekend.
wrong.why: needn't have + past participle: studied.

right: I think you should talk to your boss before you look for a new job.
You shouldn't spend so much on takeaway food.
I should have started saving money earlier.
I shouldn't have stayed up so late before my exam.

wrong.text: I think you should to speak to your manager about it.
wrong.why: should is followed by the base verb without to.

wrong.text: You should have tell me you were coming.
wrong.why: should have + past participle: told.

wrong.text: Mia is an excellent cook, so the dinner shouldn't be delicious.
wrong.why: A good cook makes us expect a good dinner: should, not shouldn't.

right: I suggest you should start with the old market.
I recommend that you take the boat trip in the evening.
It's important that everyone should arrive on time for meetings.
It's essential that new staff should read the safety rules.

wrong.text: The trainer suggested me to stretch before every run.
wrong.why: Not 'suggest somebody to do': suggest that + subject + should + base verb.

wrong.text: It's essential that every student to bring a calculator.
wrong.why: After it's essential that + subject, use should + base verb, not to + verb.

wrong.text: My sister suggested to go to the lake for the day.
wrong.why: With no person after suggest, use -ing, not to + verb.

right: You'd better take a jacket, or you'll freeze on the way home.
We'd better not leave the bikes outside because it is going to rain.
It's time I sorted out my old photos.
It's about time my brother learned to cook.

wrong.text: You'd better to take a map with you.
wrong.why: had better is followed by the base verb without to.

wrong.text: I believe every child had better learn to swim.
wrong.why: A general opinion, not one particular situation: should.

wrong.text: It's time for us went home.
wrong.why: After it's time for + person, use to + verb: for us to go.

right: I would be a terrible pilot because I'm afraid of heights.
I wouldn't mind being a chef, but I would hate the long hours.
Every summer we would pick berries in the forest.
On Fridays my mum would let us stay up late.

wrong.text: I'm glad I missed yesterday's meeting. I would fall asleep.
wrong.why: The meeting is in the past and I was not there: would have + past participle.

wrong.text: Viktor promised that he will help me move, but he never came.
wrong.why: After the past verb promised, will becomes would.

wrong.text: My uncle would own a boat when he lived by the coast.
wrong.why: own describes a state, not a repeated action: used to own.

right: Do you mind if I charge my phone in the kitchen?
Could you tell me the wifi password, please?
Would you like to come to the food market with us on Saturday?
Would you like to play tennis on Sunday morning?

wrong.text: May you send me the file again, please?
wrong.why: 'May you…?' is not a request. Use Can / Could / Would you…?

wrong.text: Would I use your bathroom, please?
wrong.why: 'Would I…?' does not ask for permission. Use Can / Could / May I…?

wrong.text: Do you like something to drink while you wait?
wrong.why: An offer now, not a question about general taste: Would you like…?

right: If the weather is good, I'll go cycling with my brother.
If I finish my project on Friday, I'll sleep until noon on Saturday.
If I lived in the mountains, I'd go skiing every week.
If I had a twin, we'd swap places at work.

wrong.text: If the weather will be nice on Sunday, we'll have a barbecue.
wrong.why: No will after if: if the weather is nice.

wrong.text: If I would know her address, I'd send her a card.
wrong.why: No would after if: if I knew.

wrong.text: I don't have a car. If I had one, I will drive you home.
wrong.why: If + past (had) goes with would, not will.

right: If I were you, I'd talk to your manager before you decide.
If I were you, I wouldn't lend him any more money.
I wish I had more time for my hobbies.
I wish I could speak French as well as my sister.

wrong.text: If I would have more time, I'd read a lot more.
wrong.why: No would in the if-part: if I had.

wrong.text: I wish I have a car. The buses here are terrible.
wrong.why: After wish we use the past: I wish I had.

wrong.text: If I would be taller, I could reach the top shelf.
wrong.why: No would in the if-part: if I were taller.

right: If I had set two alarms, I wouldn't have missed my flight.
If we'd checked the forecast, we would have taken raincoats.
I wish I had started learning the piano earlier.
I wish I hadn't spent all my savings on that trip.

wrong.text: If she had told me the truth, I would have forgive her.
wrong.why: After would have we need the past participle: forgiven.

wrong.text: I wish I didn't say that to her yesterday. She's still upset.
wrong.why: A regret about yesterday needs the past perfect: I wish I hadn't said.

wrong.text: I wish I would have brought a warmer jacket.
wrong.why: Not would have after wish: I wish I had brought.

right: I wish my neighbours wouldn't park in front of our gate.
I wish my laptop would start more quickly.
I hope your interview goes really well.
I hope you don't get stuck in traffic.

wrong.text: I wish you have a great holiday in Greece.
wrong.why: For a future event we want: hope + present, not wish.

wrong.text: I wish you will stop checking your phone during dinner.
wrong.why: After wish we use would, not will.

wrong.text: I wish I would speak better French.
wrong.why: Not 'I wish I would'. About yourself: I wish I could speak / I spoke.

right: My phone is made in Vietnam.
These trainers are sold all over the world.
My favourite song was written by a street musician.
Our school was designed by a famous architect.

wrong.text: The post delivers before nine every morning.
wrong.why: The post does not deliver anything; somebody delivers it: is delivered.

wrong.text: Three paintings stole from the museum last week.
wrong.why: Paintings cannot steal. They receive the action: were stolen.

wrong.text: The match watched by more than two million people.
wrong.why: The match received the action: was watched by…

right: A new supermarket is being built opposite my flat.
The road outside my house is being repaired this month.
Homework must be handed in on Mondays.
The kitchen should be cleaned after every meal.

wrong.text: All phones must switch off during the exam.
wrong.why: Phones cannot switch themselves off here: must be switched off.

wrong.text: My application has rejected twice this year.
wrong.why: The application receives the action: has been rejected.

wrong.text: The patient is been examined by the doctor now.
wrong.why: In progress now: is being examined. been is for the perfect.

right: I was given a guitar for my sixteenth birthday.
I was told to arrive ten minutes early.
I hate being woken up early at the weekend.
I remember being told off for talking in class.

wrong.text: Every new employee gives a laptop on the first day.
wrong.why: The employee receives the laptop, so the verb is passive: is given.

wrong.text: I am born in a hospital near the sea.
wrong.why: Your birth is in the past: I was born.

wrong.text: I wasn't get paid last month.
wrong.why: get forms its negative with didn't: I didn't get paid.

right: The old tower in my town is said to be haunted.
That footballer is believed to earn a million a week.
I'm supposed to finish my project by Friday.
We're not supposed to bring food into the classroom.

wrong.text: There is reported that three climbers are missing.
wrong.why: This pattern always starts with It: It is reported that…

wrong.text: She is said earning more than the director.
wrong.why: After is said we use to + infinitive, not -ing.

wrong.text: We supposed to hand in the essay tomorrow.
wrong.why: The form needs be: we are supposed to…

right: I had my phone screen replaced last week.
I'm getting my hair cut on Saturday.
My brother had his bike stolen outside the cinema.
We had our flight cancelled because of fog.

wrong.text: We had the carpets clean before we moved in.
wrong.why: After the object we need the past participle: cleaned.

wrong.text: We are have a new shower installed next week.
wrong.why: An arrangement for the future: we are having + object + past participle.

wrong.text: She had her passport steal at the airport.
wrong.why: After the object we need the past participle: stolen.

right: My sister said that she was looking for a new flat.
My friend said he couldn't come to the match.
My brother said he would fix my bike.
The plumber said he would come the next day.

wrong.text: The receptionist said the gym is closed that evening, so we left.
wrong.why: The evening is over, so the verb must move back: is → was.

wrong.text: The mechanic said the car will be ready by five, but it wasn't.
wrong.why: will becomes would in reported speech.

wrong.text: In May Luca said he would phone me tomorrow, but he never did.
wrong.fix: the next day / the following day
wrong.why: Reported much later, tomorrow becomes the next day.

right: My manager told me to answer every email the same day.
My dad told me not to leave my bike outside.
I told my friend that I don't drink coffee.
I said that I work on Saturdays.

wrong.text: When I met Eva in 2019, she said she is twenty-five.
wrong.why: Her age then is no longer true, so: was.

wrong.text: 'It rained all night.' 'Was it? I didn't hear anything.'

wrong.text: Let's order a pizza, will we?
wrong.why: After Let's… the tag is shall we?

I keep putting off tidying my wardrobe.

wrong.text: I can't imagine to work without a computer.
wrong.why: imagine + -ing: imagine working.

wrong.text: He has put off to go to the dentist for months.
wrong.why: put off + -ing: put off going.

wrong.text: I'm considering to not go to the wedding.
wrong.why: consider + -ing, and the negative is not + -ing: considering not going.

right: I hope to pass my driving test before the summer.
I've decided not to buy a new phone this year.
I don't know what to cook for my parents on Sunday.
I can't decide whether to change my job.

wrong.text: Marta offered driving me to the airport.
wrong.why: offer + to: offered to drive.

wrong.text: The children pretended being asleep when I looked in.
wrong.why: pretend + to: pretended to be asleep.

wrong.text: I didn't know what say when she started crying.
wrong.why: Question word + to + verb: what to say.

right: My sister wants me to help her move next weekend.
My manager expects us to answer emails within a day.
My parents made me tidy my room every Saturday.
My mum didn't let me watch TV before school.

wrong.text: My boss wants that I work this Saturday.

wrong.text: The bad weather forced us cancelling the picnic.
wrong.why: force + object + to + verb.

wrong.text: The teacher made the whole class to stay behind after the lesson.
wrong.why: make + object + base verb, without to.

right: I remember falling off my bike in front of the whole street.
I remember visiting my grandmother every Sunday.
I must remember to renew my passport this week.
I regret not going to my friend's birthday party.

wrong.text: I remember to go to the seaside every summer as a child.
wrong.why: A memory of the past: remember + -ing.

wrong.text: Could you stop to tap your pen on the desk, please?
wrong.why: End the activity: stop + -ing.

wrong.text: Although her eyes hurt, she went on to stare at the screen for another hour.
wrong.why: The same activity continued: go on + -ing.

right: Try turning your phone off an hour before bed.
Have you tried making a shopping list before you go out?
The kitchen floor needs washing.
My bike tyres need pumping up.

wrong.text: I tried open the jar, but the lid was too tight.
wrong.why: An attempt: try + to + verb, never the bare verb.

wrong.text: The fridge is empty, so I need going to the supermarket.
wrong.why: A person needs to do something: need + to.

wrong.text: My brother helped me choosing a new laptop.
wrong.why: help + object + (to) + base verb, not -ing.

right: I'd love to see the northern lights one day.
I'd hate to work night shifts.
I like to check my bank account once a week.
I like to iron my clothes the night before.

wrong.text: We really enjoyed to walk along the river last night.
wrong.why: enjoy + -ing, never to.

wrong.text: I'd like speaking to the manager, please.
wrong.why: would like + to + verb.

wrong.text: Good evening. I like to book a table for tonight, please.
wrong.why: A wish on this occasion needs would like, not like.

right: I prefer cooking at home to eating in restaurants.
I prefer the mountains to the seaside.
I'd rather stay in and watch a film than go to a club.
I'd rather you chose the restaurant this time.

wrong.text: I prefer cycling than driving in the city.
wrong.why: prefer A to B, not than.

wrong.text: I'd rather to have a salad than a burger.
wrong.why: would rather + base verb, without to.

wrong.text: I'd rather you will call me after six this evening.
wrong.why: would rather + person + past simple, even for the future.

right: I'm quite good at fixing things around the house.

wrong.text: He's really keen on learn to sail.
wrong.why: keen on + -ing.

wrong.text: I usually have a shower before go to bed.
wrong.why: before + -ing.

wrong.text: We look forward to receive your reply.
wrong.why: look forward to + -ing.

right: I'm used to getting up at five because my shift starts at six.
I'm used to the noise of the trams outside my window.
I used to drive everywhere, but I'm getting used to taking the bus.
I used to live with my parents, and it took me a year to get used to cooking for myself.

wrong.text: I've lived here for ten years, so I'm used to deal with tourists.
wrong.why: After be used to, the verb takes -ing: dealing.

wrong.text: It took us a while to get used to live without a car.
wrong.why: After get used to, the verb takes -ing: living.

wrong.text: We used to going camping every August when the kids were small.
wrong.why: A past habit takes used to + base verb: go.

right: I'm looking forward to visiting my sister in June.
I'm thinking of joining a climbing club.

wrong.why: insist on + -ing, not insist to do.

right: The castle is worth visiting, but the café next to it is not worth trying.
That series isn't worth watching after the second season.
I spend too much time scrolling through my phone.
I have trouble getting up on Monday mornings.

wrong.why: worth is followed by -ing, not to + verb.

right: I went to the post office to collect a parcel.
I went to my sister's for dinner.
I leave the hall light on so that my daughter can find the bathroom.

wrong.why: Purpose with a verb is to + verb, not for + verb.

wrong.text: We went to the mountains to a short holiday.
wrong.why: Before a noun the purpose is for: for a short holiday.

wrong.text: Yesterday we left early so that we will avoid the traffic.
wrong.why: After a past main verb, so that takes would, not will.

right: It was kind of my aunt to lend me her car.

wrong.text: It's a big match, so the stadium is certain being full.
wrong.why: certain + to + verb, not -ing.

right: I'm afraid to cycle in the city because I'm afraid of being hit by a car.

I'm sorry for forgetting to call you back on Friday.

The last few weeks at my old job seemed endless.

wrong.text: She has long and black hair.
wrong.why: No 'and' between fact adjectives before a noun: long black hair.

wrong.text: The flowers in the hall smell beautifully.
wrong.why: After smell we use an adjective: beautiful.

wrong.text: The first few minutes of the film seemed very slowly.
wrong.why: After seem we use an adjective: slow. The first few minutes is correct.

right: My dad is a careful driver, and he always parks perfectly.
My sister is a quick learner and speaks Spanish fluently.
The café was surprisingly quiet for a Saturday.
The staff were extremely helpful and the room was reasonably cheap.

wrong.text: Please read the instructions careful before you start.
wrong.why: It says how to read, so we need an adverb: carefully.

wrong.text: The teacher answered my question friendly.
wrong.why: friendly is not an adverb. Say: in a friendly way.

wrong.text: The flat was surprising cheap for the city centre.
wrong.why: Before the adjective cheap we use an adverb: surprisingly.

right: My brother cooks really well, but he works too hard.
I swim well, but I can't run fast.
I hardly ever eat breakfast on weekdays.
I've got hardly any free time this month.

wrong.text: The whole class did very good in the test.
wrong.why: It says how the class did, so we need the adverb well.

wrong.text: She can type really fastly.
wrong.why: The adverb of fast is fast. There is no word fastly.

wrong.text: There was hardly no traffic this morning.
wrong.why: hardly is already negative: hardly any, not hardly no.

right: The pizza was so good that I ordered another one.
It was such a hot day that we stayed in the water for hours.
I haven't seen my grandmother for such a long time.
My best friend lives such a long way from here.

wrong.text: We had so nice weather on holiday.
wrong.why: weather is a noun, so we need such: such nice weather.

wrong.text: It was so a hot day that we stayed indoors.
wrong.why: There is a noun (day), so: such a hot day that …

wrong.text: We walked so a long way that my feet hurt.
wrong.why: With the noun way we need such: such a long way.

right: I was too tired to go to the gym yesterday.
I didn't have enough time to finish the report.
There are too many cars in my street.
There aren't enough parks in my town.

wrong.text: We don't have enough of time to visit the museum.
wrong.why: enough goes directly before a noun, with no of: enough time.

wrong.text: I couldn't sleep because there was too many noise.
wrong.why: noise is uncountable here, so: too much noise.

wrong.text: The film was too long to watch it in one evening.
wrong.why: The film is already the object of watch, so we do not add it.

right: It's quite a warm day for October.
We stayed in a pretty noisy hotel.
I'm quite sure I locked the door this morning.
I'm not quite ready for the exam yet.

wrong.text: I pretty like my new job.
wrong.why: Before a verb we use quite, not pretty: I quite like it.

wrong.text: The news was fairly a shock to everyone.
wrong.why: Before a + noun we can use quite or rather, but not fairly: rather a shock.

wrong.text: I very agree with what you said.
wrong.why: Before agree we use quite (= completely), not very: I quite agree.

right: My home town is smaller and cheaper than the capital.
The café near my office is more expensive than the one at the station.
I drive more carefully than I did five years ago.
My English is better than it was five years ago.

wrong.text: Life in a village is peacefuler than life in the city.
wrong.why: Adjectives ending in -ful take more: more peaceful.

wrong.text: The second hotel was even worst than the first.
wrong.why: The comparative of bad is worse. worst is the superlative.

wrong.text: This café is more cheaper than the one on the corner.
wrong.why: Do not use more and -er together: cheaper.

right: My neighbourhood is a lot noisier than it was five years ago.
The buses are a bit more reliable now.
The more I cook, the more I enjoy it.
The later I go to bed, the worse I feel in the morning.

wrong.text: The exam was very easier than I expected.
wrong.why: Not very + comparative. Use much, a lot or far: much easier.

wrong.text: The longer I waited, the most impatient I became.
wrong.why: the + comparative in both halves: the longer…, the more impatient….

wrong.text: My grandmother is ten years elder than my grandfather.
wrong.why: elder cannot be used before than. Say older than.

right: I'm not as tidy as my sister.
I get up as early as my mum does.
My rent is twice as high as it was five years ago.
I don't have as many free evenings as I had last year.

wrong.text: Your coffee isn't as strong than mine.
wrong.why: as … as, not as … than.

wrong.text: We live in the same street like my grandparents.
wrong.why: the same … as, not like.

wrong.text: They arrived earlier than we were.
wrong.why: arrived is past simple, so the verb after than we is did.

right: The best concert I've ever been to was in a tiny bar.
It's the spiciest dish I've ever tried.
My aunt is the best cook in our family.
December is the busiest month of the year at my work.

wrong.text: This is the most cheap hotel in the area.
wrong.why: cheap is a short adjective: the cheapest.

wrong.text: He is one of the richest man in the country.
wrong.why: one of the + superlative + plural noun: men.

wrong.text: He's the nicest person I've never worked with.
wrong.why: After a superlative use ever, not never.

right: I like my new job very much.
I enjoyed the book you gave me very much.
I go to the swimming pool every Thursday.
On Sundays I drive to my parents' house.

wrong.text: My neighbour speaks Spanish very good.
wrong.why: After verb + object we need an adverb: speaks Spanish very well.

wrong.text: We went to there last summer.
wrong.why: No to before there. The order is right: place (there), then time (last summer).

wrong.text: At last night we stayed at home and watched a film.
wrong.why: No preposition before last night. The time expression can start the sentence.

right: I always check my phone before I get out of bed.
I've never missed a flight.
I'll probably visit my grandparents on Sunday.
I probably won't go out on Saturday night.

wrong.text: She always forget my birthday.
wrong.why: An adverb before the verb does not change it: she always forgets.

wrong.text: My parents have always live in the same village.
wrong.why: An adverb after have does not change the form: have always lived.

wrong.text: My two brothers are all taller than me.
wrong.why: Two people: both, not all.

right: I don't play computer games any more.
I no longer take the bus to work.
I've already paid the rent, but I haven't done the shopping yet.
I've already finished my essay, but I haven't sent it yet.

wrong.text: The lift yet doesn't work, so we used the stairs.
wrong.why: Before a negative verb we use still, not yet: still doesn't work.

wrong.text: I haven't decided already where to go on holiday.
wrong.why: In a negative sentence we use yet, not already.

wrong.text: She no more works at the hospital.
wrong.why: In mid-position we say no longer, not no more.

right: My grandfather is 85 and he even goes skiing.
My brother is so shy that he doesn't even answer the phone.
Even though I hate getting up early, I go running at six.
I'll go to the match even if it snows.

wrong.text: He is mad about football. He even watch the under-12 matches.
wrong.why: even before the verb does not change it: he even watches.

wrong.text: The sequel is even bad than the original.
wrong.why: even + comparative: even worse than.

wrong.text: Even I had studied all week, I failed the test.
wrong.why: even alone cannot join two clauses: Even though I had studied….

right: Although I was exhausted, I went to my friend's birthday party.
I cycled to work even though it was snowing.
Despite the terrible weather, we had a great weekend at the coast.
I passed the exam in spite of feeling nervous.

wrong.text: Despite she speaks three languages, she can't find a job.
wrong.why: Before a subject + verb (she speaks) use although, not despite.

wrong.text: We had a great holiday despite of the weather.
wrong.why: Despite is never followed by of.

wrong.text: We got home late because of the last bus didn't turn up.
wrong.why: Before a clause use because. Because of needs a noun.

right: I'll take a power bank in case my phone dies.
I'm going to pack a raincoat in case the weather changes.
I took some snacks in case the journey took longer than expected.
I saved the document three times in case my computer crashed.

wrong.text: I'll leave a key with the neighbours in case you will arrive before me.
wrong.why: No will after in case: in case you arrive.

wrong.text: Dana charged her phone before the trip in case there would be no sockets on the train.
wrong.why: No would after in case: in case there were no sockets.

wrong.text: We'll go skiing next weekend in case there's enough snow.
wrong.why: Skiing depends on the snow. That is a condition, not a precaution: if.

right: I'll go running tomorrow morning unless it's pouring with rain.
We're eating out on Friday unless I have to work late.
You can borrow my camera as long as you bring it back on Sunday.
You can use my desk provided that you don't move my papers.

wrong.text: Unless you don't leave now, you'll miss the train.
wrong.why: Unless already means "if not", so the verb after it stays positive here.

wrong.text: You can go out tonight provided you will be home by eleven.
wrong.why: Provided + present tense, not will: provided you are home.

wrong.text: You can borrow the car unless you fill up the tank afterwards.
wrong.why: Filling the tank is the condition for borrowing, so: as long as or provided.

right: Just as I was leaving the house, it started to pour.
As I got on the bus, I realised I had left my wallet at home.
As it was raining, I took the bus instead of cycling.
As I had no food at home, I ordered a pizza.

wrong.text: During I was parking the car, I scratched the door.
wrong.why: During needs a noun. Before a subject + verb use as (or while).

wrong.text: When the weeks went by, I felt more and more at home.
wrong.why: Two things changed together over time, so: as, not when.

wrong.text: As I was a teenager, I played the drums in a band.
wrong.why: For a period of your life use when. As + a state would mean because.

right: My aunt worked as a nurse for thirty years.
I spent one summer working as a tour guide.
Our classroom is so cold that it is like a fridge.
My little brother eats like a horse.

wrong.text: Their dog is huge. It is as a small horse.
wrong.why: Similar to a horse, not really a horse: like + noun.

wrong.text: My new boss is very relaxed, just as my old one.
wrong.why: Only a noun phrase follows, with no verb, so we need like.

wrong.text: She was described like a quiet, hard-working student.
wrong.why: describe somebody as + noun.

right: My brother looks as if he hasn't slept all week.
You sound as if you have had good news.
My cat behaves as if she owned the whole flat.
My little sister talks as if she were my mother.

wrong.text: It looks as it is going to snow tonight.
wrong.why: Before a clause we need as if, as though or (informal) like, not as alone.

wrong.text: The cake looked wonderful, but it tasted as cardboard.
wrong.why: taste + like + noun.

wrong.text: He walks around the office as if he be the manager.
wrong.why: Not real: as if he were (or was) the manager.

right: I stayed with my cousins for a week during the summer.
It rained for two days during our trip to the coast.
I'll feed your cat while you are away.
I'll collect your post while you're in Spain.

wrong.text: She worked in Canada during five years before coming home.
wrong.why: Five years is a length of time, so: for.

wrong.text: Please keep your seat belt fastened during we are taking off.
wrong.why: A subject and a verb follow, so we need while.

wrong.text: I'll look after your cat while you will be in hospital.
wrong.why: No will after while: while you are in hospital.

right: I have to pay the rent by the first of the month.
I need to finish my project by Friday afternoon.
By the time I got to the station, the train had left.
By the time we found the restaurant, the kitchen had closed.

wrong.text: Applications must reach us until 31 May.
wrong.why: A deadline, not later than 31 May: by.

wrong.text: By the time the guests will arrive, everything will be ready.
wrong.why: No will after by the time: by the time the guests arrive.

wrong.text: Wait here by I come back with the tickets.
wrong.why: Waiting continues up to that moment: until.

wrong.text: The builders promised to finish the roof till the end of the month.
wrong.why: Finishing is a single event with a deadline: by.

right: I have a guitar lesson at five o'clock on Thursdays.
On Saturday mornings I go to the market at about nine.
I started this job in 2022, and next month I'm changing teams.
We moved here in the spring, and every Sunday we explore a new area.

wrong.text: Sorry, Mr Okafor is in a meeting in the moment.
wrong.why: The fixed phrase is at the moment (= now).

wrong.text: The company moved to Leeds on 2015.
wrong.why: A year takes in.

wrong.text: I have a driving lesson on this afternoon.
wrong.why: No preposition before this: this afternoon.

right: I got to the station just in time to catch the last train.
I finished my essay in time, but only because I stayed up all night.
At first I wanted to study law, but in the end I chose design.
At first we couldn't find a flat we liked. In the end we found one near the park.

wrong.text: Our flight left exactly in time, at 10.40.
wrong.why: It left at the planned time, so: on time.

wrong.text: Sign your name in the end of the form, please.
wrong.why: With of + noun we say at the end of, never in the end of.

wrong.text: In first I thought the message was a joke.
wrong.why: The phrase is at first (= in the early stage).

right: My laptop is on the desk and my headphones are in the top drawer.
There is a calendar on the wall and a pile of books in a box.
My flat is on the second floor, at the end of the corridor.
Our office is on the left, at the top of the stairs.

wrong.text: My aunt has a tiny flat at Madrid.
wrong.why: A city is a space you are inside: in Madrid.

wrong.text: The toilets are in the end of the corridor.
wrong.why: The end of something is a point: at the end of the corridor.

wrong.text: The accounts department is in the ground floor.
wrong.why: Floors of a building take on: on the ground floor.

right: My mum is at work and my brother is still in bed.
My dad is at a friend's house and my sister is in her room.
I listen to podcasts on the bus every morning.
On the way to college I always buy a coffee.

wrong.text: I like the way the artist uses light on this picture.
wrong.why: What you see is in a picture, not on it.

wrong.text: Leila met her husband on a friend's wedding.
wrong.why: An event takes at: at a wedding.

wrong.text: Write your address in the back of the envelope, please.
wrong.why: The back of an envelope is a surface: on the back.

right: I saw two of my old classmates at a concert last month.
There was amazing food at my cousin's wedding.
We arrived in Prague early in the morning.
I arrived at the airport three hours before my flight.

wrong.text: We missed you in Omar's leaving party on Friday.
wrong.why: A party is an event: at a party.

wrong.text: My best friend has lived at Manchester since she was a child.
wrong.why: People live in a city: in Manchester.

wrong.text: We arrived to the hotel just before dinner.
wrong.why: Never arrive to. A hotel is a building: arrive at the hotel.

right: It takes me forty minutes to get to work, and I get home at about seven.
I get to college in twenty minutes, but I never get home before six.
I've been to Turkey twice, but I've never been to Istanbul.
I'd love to go to Iceland one day.

wrong.text: Last summer we went in Greece for the first time.
wrong.why: Go is a verb of movement: went to Greece.

wrong.text: I'm tired. Let's go to home.
wrong.why: Go home takes no preposition.

wrong.text: I got on the car and realised I had left my phone in the house.
wrong.why: We get in or into a car, not on it.

right: I learned to ride a bike at the age of six.
My brother moved abroad at the age of twenty-two.
When we were on holiday in Greece, we spent every afternoon in the shade.
On a trip to Edinburgh I walked for hours in the rain.

wrong.text: On my opinion, we should wait until the spring.
wrong.why: The fixed phrase is in my opinion.

wrong.text: We met a lovely couple from Chile while we were in holiday.
wrong.why: The fixed phrase is on holiday.

wrong.text: She became a professor in the age of 29.
wrong.why: Age takes at: at the age of 29.

right: I usually go to work by bus, but on Fridays I go on foot.
We do the weekly shopping by car.
I sent a message to the wrong person by mistake.
I left my keys at the office by accident.

wrong.text: I think my brother broke my headphones by purpose.
wrong.why: By mistake and by accident, but on purpose.

wrong.text: We decided to go with car because there were five of us.
wrong.why: How we travel: by car, not with car.

wrong.text: The glass was cut by an expert by a special tool.
wrong.why: The expert is the doer (by); the tool takes with.

right: The main cause of the traffic jams in my town is the narrow bridge.
Nobody has found a solution to the parking problem near my office.
The main difference between my two jobs is the number of meetings.
One advantage of my old phone was its battery.

wrong.text: What was the reason of your decision to leave?
wrong.why: We say a reason for something, not a reason of.

wrong.text: Nobody has found the key from the storage room.
wrong.why: We say the key to a door or a room.

wrong.text: We have very little contact to our head office.
wrong.why: We say contact with somebody or something.

right: It was kind of my neighbour to water my plants while I was away.
It was generous of my colleague to share her notes with me.
I'm excited about my cousin's wedding next month.
I'm fed up with the roadworks outside my flat.

wrong.text: It was nice from you to remember my birthday.
wrong.why: We say it was nice of somebody to do something, not from.

wrong.text: Our teacher was angry on us for being late again.
wrong.why: Angry with a person for doing something.

wrong.text: I'm really sorry of the noise last night.
wrong.why: Sorry about or for something, never sorry of.

right: I'm good at fixing computers but hopeless at cooking.
I'm quite good at languages, but I'm hopeless at remembering dates.
My city is famous for its old bridges.
In summer the centre is crowded with tourists.

wrong.text: He's jealous on his sister because she earns more.
wrong.why: Jealous of somebody.

wrong.text: Their new flat is very different of the old one.
wrong.why: Different from something, not different of.

wrong.text: The streets were crowded of people selling souvenirs.
wrong.why: Crowded with people, but full of people.

right: My sister phoned the shop and explained the problem to the manager.
The waiter apologised to us, and we thanked him for the free dessert.
A boy threw the ball to his friend, and everyone looked at them.
A driver shouted at a cyclist who had crossed in front of him.

wrong.text: I usually listen at podcasts while I'm cooking.
wrong.why: We listen to something or somebody.

wrong.text: I phoned to the dentist and made an appointment.
wrong.why: Phone takes an object directly: phone somebody, not phone to somebody.

wrong.text: Don't throw stones to the ducks. You'll hurt them.
wrong.why: Throw something at somebody or something when the aim is to hit.

right: I'm looking for a flat closer to my office.
I applied for a summer job at a hotel last week.
My grandmother looks after my little brother after school.
I take care of the plants on our balcony.

wrong.text: We discussed about the price for nearly an hour.
wrong.why: Discuss takes an object directly: discuss something.

wrong.text: She left Madrid to Lisbon last night.
wrong.why: Leave one place for another place.

wrong.text: I'm looking after my keys. Have you seen them anywhere?
wrong.why: You are trying to find them, so: look for.

right: The smell of rain reminds me of my summers in the village.
This song reminds me of my last year at school.
I need to think about the job offer before I answer.
I can't think of a good present for my sister.

wrong.text: I haven't heard of my sister since Friday. She isn't answering her phone.
wrong.why: No message or call from her: hear from somebody.

wrong.text: I recognise that actor, but I can't think about his name.
wrong.why: Remember a name = think of it.

wrong.text: That smell reminds me about my school canteen.
wrong.why: It makes me remember, so: reminds me of.

right: I thanked my neighbour for looking after my cat.
I apologised for being late to the meeting.
My holiday plans depend on how much money I save.
It depends on the weather, but I want to go hiking.

wrong.text: The writer died by a rare illness at the age of forty.
wrong.why: Die of or from an illness, not die by.

wrong.text: My sister thanked me about the flowers I sent.
wrong.why: Thank somebody for something.

wrong.text: We congratulated them with the birth of their daughter.
wrong.why: Congratulate somebody on something, not with.

right: I spend most of my money on rent and food.
I spend too much time on my phone in the evening.
I prefer trains to buses because I can read.
I prefer cooking at home to eating out.

wrong.text: Nobody succeeded to find a cheaper flight.
wrong.why: Succeed is followed by in + -ing.

wrong.text: I prefer walking than taking the bus.
wrong.why: Prefer one thing to another, not than.

wrong.text: I can never concentrate in my homework when the TV is on.
wrong.why: Concentrate on something.

right: I'm looking forward to my sister's wedding in June.
I'm really looking forward to seeing my old school friends.
The TV is too loud, so I'm going to turn it down.
These shoes hurt, so I'll take them off.

wrong.text: The plane took up on time and landed in Rome at noon.
wrong.why: A plane takes off (= leaves the ground).

wrong.text: It was freezing outside, so I put my gloves up.
wrong.why: put on clothes = dress yourself in them.

wrong.text: I'm looking forward to meet your family.
wrong.why: After look forward to we use -ing, not the infinitive.

right: We checked in at about three and went straight to the beach.
I had to check out before ten, so I got up early.
I tried to get out of going to the dentist, but my mum insisted.
I couldn't get out of giving a speech at my friend's wedding.

wrong.text: If you're ever in our area, please drop on for a coffee.
wrong.why: drop in = visit somebody for a short time without arranging it.

wrong.text: We paid the bill and checked off of the hotel at ten.
wrong.why: check out of a hotel = pay and leave.

wrong.text: He always finds a way to get out of wash the dishes.
wrong.why: get out of + -ing.

right: I expected a boring evening, but it turned out to be great fun.
The restaurant looked expensive, but it turned out that the prices were fine.
We have run out of coffee again.
I often run out of battery by the evening.

wrong.text: Don't forget to put off your campfire before you leave.
wrong.why: put out a fire = make it stop burning. (put off = postpone.)

wrong.text: A volunteer stood at the door and gave off leaflets.
wrong.why: give out = give one to each person.

wrong.text: I've fallen out of my cousin, so I'm not going to his party.
wrong.why: fall out with somebody.

right: I keep putting off cleaning the windows.
I've put off my visit to the dentist until next month.
We set off at five in the morning to catch the ferry.
My best friend came to the station to see me off.

wrong.text: I can't see anything. Can you turn the lamp in?
wrong.why: turn on a lamp = make it start working.

wrong.text: They had to call out the open-air concert when the storm began.
wrong.why: call off an event = cancel it.

wrong.text: I tried up three dresses, but none of them fitted.
wrong.why: try on clothes = put them on to see if they fit.

right: My dad told me off for breaking the window.
The teacher told me off because I had forgotten my homework again.
My brother keeps on leaving his shoes in the hall.
I carried on reading until two in the morning.

wrong.text: She keeps on to ask me the same question.
wrong.why: keep on + -ing, not the infinitive.

wrong.text: He was so tired that he dozed out in the armchair.
wrong.why: doze off = fall asleep.

wrong.text: Children often show out when visitors come.
wrong.why: show off = try to get attention and admiration.

right: I'm trying to cut down on sweet drinks.
I should cut down on the time I spend on my phone.
Our washing machine broke down just before the holidays.
My friend let me down when he forgot my birthday.

wrong.text: I need a hammer and a nail to put on this picture.
wrong.why: put up a picture = fix it on the wall.

wrong.text: You eat too many sweets. You should cut down of them.
wrong.why: cut down on something.

wrong.text: The factory closed off two years ago and has been empty since then.
wrong.why: close down = stop doing business for ever.

right: I grew up in a small town near the sea.
I was brought up by my parents and my grandmother.
We wanted to go to the beach, but we ended up watching films at home.
I went in for one book and ended up buying five.

wrong.text: Wages are not keeping up to prices this year.
wrong.why: keep up with something = rise or move as fast as it.

wrong.text: I brought up in a village, so I love the countryside.
wrong.why: Children grow up (no object) or are brought up (passive).

wrong.text: After the party we stayed behind to tidy down the hall.
wrong.why: tidy up = make a place neat.

right: I have to put up with my neighbour's loud music.
I can't put up with slow internet when I'm working.
My friends took me out for pizza to cheer me up.
I cheered up when I heard the good news.

wrong.text: Our manager came up for a clever plan to cut costs.
wrong.why: come up with a plan = think of it.

wrong.text: The gas bottle blew down and destroyed the garage.
wrong.why: blow up = explode.

wrong.text: The twins look so alike that I always mix them out.
wrong.why: mix up = think that one person or thing is another.

right: My sister borrowed my charger and never gave it back.
I paid my friend back the next day.
I threw away all my old school notebooks.
I gave my old bike away to a neighbour.

wrong.text: Keep away of the fire, children!
wrong.why: keep away from something.

wrong.text: I left two messages, but he never rang me away.
wrong.why: ring somebody back = return their phone call.

wrong.text: When I look back of my student years, I mostly remember the fun.
wrong.why: look back on a time in your past.

right: I'm a student from Russia.
I'm twenty-two years old.
My mother is a doctor.
My friends are very funny.

wrong.text: My mother are a teacher.
wrong.why: My mother = she, so we use is.

wrong.text: My brothers is at school.
wrong.why: My brothers = they, so are.

wrong.text: He're my best friend.
wrong.why: he + is = he's.

right: I'm not at work today.
My brother isn't a student.
Where is your office?
How old is your sister?

wrong.text: My friends isn't from here.
wrong.why: My friends = they, so aren't.

wrong.text: Is your parents at home?
wrong.why: Your parents = they, so Are.

wrong.text: Where are your school?
wrong.why: Your school = it, so is.

right: This is my old phone.
These pens are new.
That car is very old.
Those trees are very tall.

wrong.text: This man over there is my teacher.
wrong.why: Over there = far, so that.

wrong.text: This shoes are too small.
wrong.why: Shoes = many, so these.

wrong.text: What is those boxes?
wrong.why: Those boxes = many, so are.

right: My mother is a nurse.
My uncle is an engineer.
I have two chairs in my room.
There are three windows in my room.

wrong.text: He is a engineer.
wrong.why: Engineer starts with e, so we use an.

wrong.text: My friend has three dog at home.
wrong.why: Three = many, so add -s.

wrong.text: My foots are very cold.
wrong.why: Foot → feet. No -s.

right: My brother and his wife have two children.
My mother loves her garden.
This is my sister's laptop.
